title: Can Trust in Science Be Improved? An Adaptive Experiment Testing Student-Designed Messages
summary: Can brief, student-designed messages raise trust in science? We ran a registered online survey experiment with US adults recruited through Lucid, randomly assigning respondents to one of 32 messages (videos, texts, memes, posters and infographics) or a pure control that only asked them to continue. Of 11,519 raw responses, 8,572 were analysed. Trust in science was measured after treatment on a scale where the control mean was 3.685. One video, 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?', lowered trust by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' clip lowered it by 0.104 points. Three videos raised trust by roughly 0.06 points each: the peer-review video and two student-made videos. For the other arms the results were inconclusive; their intervals were wide and do not

extensions.label: Design advance
extensions.why: Addresses power and measurement. It concentrates the sample on the two best-supported arms plus the peer-review video, tests them against control in a confirmatory design, and adds a delayed and a behavioural outcome.
extensions.title: Replicating the short student videos with a delayed follow-up and a behavioural outcome
extensions.hypothesis: Each video raises immediate trust relative to control (position a). Under position b, contrasts are near zero after Holm correction. Effects at 7 days are smaller than or equal to immediate effects.
extensions.primary_outcome: Immediate post-treatment trust in science (mean of 6 items, items 4-6 reverse-coded), with 7-day trust and the behavioural choice as secondary outcomes.

extensions.label: Generalizability
extensions.why: Addresses the missing moderator and the sample. The exploratory interaction of 0.165 in the Science in everyday life arm is untested confirmatory, and partisan effects bear on where the result holds.
extensions.title: Does partisanship moderate the student-video effect?
extensions.hypothesis: The video raises trust more among Republican-leaning respondents than among non-Republicans (positive interaction). Under the null (position b) the interaction and the main effect are near zero.
extensions.primary_outcome: Trust in science: mean of the 6 post-treatment items, items 4-6 reverse-coded.

extensions.label: Theoretical debate
extensions.why: Addresses design confounding. It tests whether the small gains reflect content or merely an attention cue, which discriminates between the brief-messages-work and beliefs-resist positions.
extensions.title: Format versus content: separating persuasion from salience
extensions.hypothesis: If content drives the effect (position a), only the two science-framing cells raise trust relative to control and neutral cells. If salience or format alone drives it, neutral cells also move trust. If beliefs resist (position b), all contrasts are near zero.
extensions.primary_outcome: Post-treatment trust in science (mean of the 6 items, items 4-6 reverse-coded), adjusted for pre-trust.

potential.verdict: A follow-up is worth running, but a narrow one. The study's main result is that most messages do nothing detectable. Only the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video survives multiplicity, and its negative effect (-0.171) is more credible than the gains of about 0.06. Run the replication of the two student videos with a delayed and a behavioural outcome first, because it tests the only consistent positive signal at adequate power. Then run the format-versus-content test and the partisanship moderation test. The literature retrieved is thin, so the debate is only loosely anchored.
